The most important bit here is this concept: To prevent collusion against the userbase, create maximally conflicting incentive structures between all groups of concern such that they can never cooperate; never give a single iota of trust to anyone in power regardless of how much you like them personally.

First-level thoughts on implementation follow. Any holes? Please, point them out and offer patches. There need to be stable solutions, or Digg 3.0 is probably inevitable in under a decade, regardless of how nice Atko et al are.

  1. Permanent, non-removable admins must abdicate most if not all political authority. Any powers they give themselves must be symmetrically revocable by user action. If they want to give themselves authority to elect new admins by fiat, then users must have the ability to remove those admins via referendum.

  2. Admins must be removable by user action.

  3. Moderators need to live under legitimate threat of removal of their power as a consequence of user displeasure. If the first condition is followed, this power should not be given into the hands of users directly, but be an administrative function - so long as the first condition is followed, Admins and Mods have a nominally different incentive structure.

  4. To further differentiate the incentive structure, Mods must be banned from any kind of incitement/campaigning in decisions involving Admins that regular users may partake in.

  5. A person who is a Mod on any account shouldn't be an Admin on any account. If there are exceptions, they must be apolitical on the Admin side, regardless of if they are in a permanent position. They could perhaps have access to non-user-accessible functions of maintenance, but not, eg, banning or fine control of spam filters.

  6. Log everything. Probabilistically log accounts that are probably Mod/Admin Alts with assigned confidence values and some way of getting off that list through a verification process. Power must preclude privacy no matter how small that power. No exceptions for Mods of tiny subs (and I say this as one myself)

All of this requires nominal good faith from the group we call permanent admins due to Voat's centralised structure. It wouldn't work on today's Reddit; I think it might have a chance of working on today's Voat, but not if this is the end of things. Governments have been manipulating Reddit's output for years, and without a hard counter to that, eventually, this site will undergo a similar process of gentrification to what Reddit is suffering today. I don't know about you guys but personally I use Kindle Direct Publishing. I only use them because I also opt in to their select scheme. That's when you give them exclusive rights to your book in return for being able to do sales and some other nifty benefits. Because of that I'm not on Nook or anything. I don't even know how to get on to Nook but I imagine it's not too difficult. I'm with CreateSpace for physical copies of books but only one of my books has physical copies available at the minute.

So what about you? Are you with KDP? Nook? Did you go straight to CreateSpace without going through Amazon first?
What Platform Do You Publish On?

As a fairly new writer (only ~12 months under my belt and only 1 book finished with a second almost being done) I haven't have much experience in publishing yet.
That being said my first book is available on Kindle Direct Publishing, and is currently in the "Unlimited" selection. I'm fairly pleased with the way they do things, but there are some items that are starting to pull me away. I'm not a huge fan of the 70/30 royalties, especially with the 70% being limited at $9.99 max. By no means would I expect to sell my book for more than that on KDP, but I don't like that it's not an option. That and the 60 day waiting period on the money.... Other than that I love it.
For my physical publishing, I've only used BookBaby. They were recommended to me by my former composition instructor. They're decent, but, and I don't know if this is universal with publishers, they're crazy expensive. I've only ever had one issue with them; one copy of my book was printed upside down. Essentially if you opened the cover, you would be on the last page and the words were upside down. At least if I ever get famous (lol) I'll have a collector's item misprinted from first print.

I think my biggest problem with KDP when I started out was that you needed to have made $10 in royalties before they would pay you. My first book was made available for really cheap and I'd have had to have sold a lot of copies to make even ten dolalrs. They've changed that rule now though. To be honest I didn't realise there was a max price for your book. I don't expect to sell a book for over ten dollars as it is. If I did reach that point I might have to find another outlet. Or maybe they'll have changed the system by then.

If you got famous and you signed that misprinted edition it could end up being worth a lot. CreateSpace is a little expensive but I don't know how bad it is by comparison. I think that in order to get a test or promotional copy of a book I have to spend about three dollars or something. I was able to price it at about the same price, but just a dollar or two more to cover production costs.

The price cap is just a pain for anyone that wants to go over $10 (again, not me...yet). If you set it for the max ($9.99) you'd get $6.99 in royalties. BUT if you want to post it up for $10.00, you have to choose 30% royalty and you'd get $3.00. To get the $6.99 you'd have to set it to $23.30. I guess it is what it is though.
The biggest issue with Bookbaby is the 25 Copy minimum, and the fact that, for a full novel, they charge ~$13 a copy.

Yeesh that's definitely way higher than it is with CreateSpace. I think if I reached that point I'd have to just have $9.99 be the flat rate on ebooks and charge a little more on CreateSpace. I think I'd have the option to do that.
I will be trying out createspace for my next print then. Thank you for the suggestion.
